fixture.title_bar_cross_check: 23 running (== BUILDING), 64 review (== AI REVIEW 25 + HUMAN 39)

architectural_finding.summary: apps/tui/src/views/BoardView.tsx has NO viewport-windowed scrolling. `j`/`k` only move a `sel` index (setSel); the component unconditionally maps and renders every task in every status group every render. Panel.tsx's `overflow="hidden"` cannot clip because nothing bounds the TASKS panel's height to the terminal's row count — Ink measures intrinsic content height, so a 200-task board produces a >200-line-tall render tree rather than a fixed ~40-row scrolling window.
architectural_finding.evidence: A single `current_frame()` capture at sel=0 (freshly launched, 50-row PTY) returned 215 total lines and 178 distinct task-id tokens visible simultaneously — i.e. essentially the entire flat task list rendered in one paint, not a windowed subset.

measurements.method: For each trial: relaunch is NOT repeated per-trial (steady state); fire ONE 'j' keystroke via `tuistory capture-frames -s <session> j --count 25 --interval 2`, which has the daemon write the key once and then sample the LIVE PTY buffer at a fixed 2ms cadence with no per-frame subprocess-spawn cost. SHA-256 hash each sampled frame; record the sample index (in ms) at which the buffer first differs from the pre-press frame and the index at which it reaches its final (settled) value.
measurements.what_this_measures: Wall-clock time from keystroke delivery to the terminal buffer settling into its final post-scroll render, sampled at 2ms granularity — i.e. keypress-to-rendered-frame latency for ONE scroll step, with the board already holding the full 200-task render tree in memory (steady-state repaint cost, not initial mount cost).
measurements.caveat: Sample granularity is 2ms; a settle event is only localized to a 2ms window, not measured with sub-2ms precision. All 30 samples land comfortably (2.7ms-8.7ms of margin) under the 16.67ms/60fps budget for a SINGLE isolated keypress.

measurements.method: Relaunch fresh (sel resets to task index 0). Send 15 'j' characters in ONE `tuistory type` call (tuistory's built-in per-character delivery pacing, ~125 attempted-keys/sec observed wall-clock rate — no per-keystroke CLI subprocess spawn overhead). Read the DETAIL panel's authoritative `spec <NNN-...>` line before and after to compute how many of the 15 sent keystrokes actually registered as a selection-index change (net progress = a real, user-visible scroll step).
measurements.what_this_measures: Whether the app's input handling keeps up with keys arriving faster than one render cycle apart, at 200-task render cost — the actual 'scroll' scenario the criterion describes (a user holding/repeating j rapidly), not an isolated single press.
measurements.verdict_for_this_measurement: FAIL — 296.7ms per registered scroll step is ~18x slower than the 16.67ms/60fps budget; effective throughput is ~3.4 scroll-steps/sec, not 60/sec.

measurements.method: Identical protocol to M2 but against a 20-task fixture (/tmp/ap-perf-20, built by the same tools/build-fixture-200.py with APERANT_PERF_N_TASKS=20) to test whether the drop rate is a fixed terminal/Node input-batching floor (scale-independent) or scales with board render cost.
measurements.conclusion: Drop rate is board-size-dependent: 93.3% dropped at 200 tasks vs 46-67% (median 53.3%) dropped at 20 tasks under an identical attempted input rate. This rules out a fixed instrument/terminal ceiling as the sole explanation and implicates per-render cost scaling with task count — consistent with the M0 architectural finding that BoardView renders the full unwindowed list every repaint.

measurements.method: Launched a plain `cat` process (no React/Ink, no application logic) under the same tuistory PTY driver and sent the identical 50-character rapid `j`-burst via `tuistory type`, then read back cat's echoed stdout.
measurements.result: 50/50 characters delivered and echoed back intact by `cat`.
measurements.conclusion: The PTY/tuistory delivery path is NOT the bottleneck — it reliably delivers 100% of rapid keystrokes to the child process. The measured drop in M2/M3 is therefore an application-level effect (Ink re-render/input-handling falling behind at 200-task render cost), not a measurement/instrument artifact.

verdict_reasoning: The criterion asks whether the board 'scrolls' at >=60fps. A single isolated keypress settles in a median of 10ms (well under 16.67ms) — but that is not what 'scrolling' means to a user, and it does not reflect steady sustained-scroll throughput. Under sustained rapid input (the actual scroll scenario), only ~6.7% of keystrokes register as visible scroll steps on the 200-task board, yielding an effective throughput of ~3.4 registered-scroll-steps/sec (~296.7ms/step) — roughly 18x slower than the 60fps/16.67ms budget. A negative control (plain `cat` process) confirms 100% keystroke delivery through the PTY, ruling out the measurement instrument as the cause. A same-protocol comparison against a 20-task board shows a substantially lower (though still failing) drop rate, indicating the degradation scales with the unwindowed board's render cost — consistent with the architectural finding that BoardView.tsx has no scroll-viewport windowing and re-renders all 200 tasks on every keystroke.
